Bill Maher mocks Mamdani for pivoting to Israel criticism in Oct. 7 tribute, calls it 'tone deaf'

Bill Maher blasted Zohran Mamdani's Oct. 7 anniversary statement on "Real Time," mocking the New York City mayor's pivot to criticizing Israel.

Actual Article Body:

Bill Maher mocked Zohran Mamdani over his response to the third anniversary of the Oct 7 terrorist attack in Israel, joking that the New York City mayor's rap name could be 'Tone Deaf.'  (FilmMagic via Getty Images)

Comedian Bill Maher took aim at New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani over his statement marking the third anniversary of the deadly Oct. 7 Hamas terrorist attack on Israel.

Maher used Friday's episode of "Real Time" to criticize Mamdani's statement, in which the mayor called the day "profoundly painful for so many New Yorkers" and said the city grieves "alongside our many friends and neighbors who still carry that unthinkable loss."

Mamdani went on to condemn the ongoing defensive acts being carried out by Israel, writing, "The suffering did not begin nor end that day. It instead continued through the Israeli government’s devastating, ongoing genocide in Gaza, in which it has killed more than 74,000 Palestinians—including more than 21,000 children."

ISRAEL AMB TORCHES MAMDANI OCT 7 POST: 'LIKE TURNING SEPTEMBER 11 INTO A DAY OF MOURNING FOR AL-QAEDA'

An anti-Israel crowd was just outside the barricades of the Israelis for Peace Vigil, beating on drums and attempting to drown out the speakers. (CHARLY TRIBALLEAU / AFP via Getty Images)

The mayor continued, writing that "even since the so-called ceasefire, more than 1,400 Palestinians have been killed," adding "many New Yorkers are reckoning with this unbearable grief, and we mourn alongside them—all while knowing that our tax dollars fund these war crimes."

Mamdani also wrote, "Three years later, we must refuse to accept a world in which occupation and apartheid continue, where war crimes are met with impunity, and our federal government continues its complicity with every arms shipment."

SCHUMER, JEFFRIES DODGE MAMDANI CONTROVERSY AS FELLOW NEW YORK DEM UNLOADS

"To honor the dead, we must fight for a world in which every person can live with freedom, safety, and dignity," the mayor said.

Mamdani’s reaction to the anniversary did not go over well with Maher, who harshly criticized the mayor.

BILL MAHER RIPS MACKLEMORE'S GAZA STANCE, SAYS CELEBRITY 'MORAL CONFUSION' IS FUELING ANTISEMITISM

New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani speaks during a press conference at the site where a man was shot by an Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) officer during an operation in the Bronx, on October 8, 2026, in New York City. (Ryan Murphy/Getty Images)

"Mayor Mamdani, not all that sympathetic to this stuff, but he did make some nice remarks about it," Maher said, referring to Mamdani’s statement.

"But then he pivoted right to, ‘but Israel made them do it,’" Maher said, offering his interpretation of the mayor's remarks.

ANTI-ISRAEL PROTESTERS LABEL MAMDANI A 'TRAITOR,' ACCUSE HIM OF 'GENOCIDE' OUTSIDE OCT 7 VIGIL

The comedian also mocked Mamdani's past career as a rapper, during which he performed under the stage names "Young Cardamom" and "Mr. Cardamom."

"You know, he used to be a rapper. His rap name was ‘Tone Deaf,’" Maher quipped.

Mamdani also faced criticism earlier this week after dining Wednesday at Ayat Hinds Hall, a Palestinian restaurant. The restaurant's sister location drew criticism in 2023 over menu language that critics described as antisemitic.

The sister restaurant previously drew criticism after the Times of Israel reported that the front page of its menu featured the phrase "Down with the occupation" in English, Arabic and Hebrew. Owner Abdul Elenani previously said the language appeared on the menu before Hamas' Oct. 7, 2023, attack on Israel.

ANTI-ISRAEL GROUPS RALLY ACROSS US ON OCTOBER 7 ANNIVERSARY, CHANTING 'LONG LIVE THE INTIFADA'

Democratic strategist Kaivan Shroff, however, suggested that Maher's criticism could benefit Mamdani politically.

"At first glance it could appear Mamdani missed the mark with his statement or is being ‘tone-deaf’ as Maher puts it — but I’d argue it was actually a page from the Trump playbook," Shroff told Fox News Digital.

"Mamdani’s base was criticizing him for having NYPD protect Netanyahu, keeping on Commissioner Tisch, arresting protesters, not following through on his promise to disband the Strategic Response Group," Shroff continued. "And a tweet or statement that plays to what his base wants to hear, ruffles feathers, grabs headlines and earns some backlash is a way to try and placate his supporters and seem like a fighter on key campaign issues that he has actually backed away from. "

Shroff went on to suggest Maher’s criticism of Mamdani is actually helping the mayor solidify his support from those who may have questioned his commitment to his campaign promises surrounding the Israel-Hamas conflict.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE COVERAGE OF MEDIA AND CULTURE

"To that end, Maher is actually helping him in responding like this," Shroff said. "For some Mamdani fans the fact that he has enraged folks like Maher is a sign that he is still the same candidate they voted for."

CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

Fox News Digital reached out to the Mamdani administration for comment but did not receive an immediate response.

Mamdani snubs Brooklyn Columbus Day Parade, ghosts Queens organizers: ‘slap in the face’

Mayor Zohran Mamdani slapped New York’s Italian American community in the face again Saturday -- snubbing Brooklyn’s annual Columbus Day Parade and ghosting organizers of a similar event in Queens.

Actual Article Body:
Switch between CA and NY editions here.

See more of our coverage in your search results.

Mayor Zohran Mamdani slapped New York’s Italian American community in the face again Saturday — snubbing Brooklyn’s annual Columbus Day Parade and ghosting organizers of a similar event in Queens.

Members of the Federation of Italian American Organizations of Brooklyn, which organizes the parade along 18th Avenue in Bensonhurst honoring the famed but controversial explorer, said the Mayor’s Office confirmed on Thursday that Mamdani declined their invitation sent out weeks earlier.

But at least Brooklyn’s organizers got an answer.

Organizers of the annual Queens Columbus Day Parade in Astoria said the mayor never responded to an invitation to attend their parade — leaving them hanging as it concluded Saturday near the Columbus statue by Astoria Boulevard, the same monument Mamdani famously flipped the bird to in 2020.

And the mayor is also unlikely to attend the larger Columbus Day Parade in Manhattan on Monday, sources said.

The Columbus Citizens Foundation, which runs the famed parade along Fifth Avenue, got plenty of heat from other Italian American groups for trying to extend an olive branch to Mamdani by inviting him to the event despite the socialist mayor’s past rocky relationship with Italian Americans.

Christopher Loiacono, president of the Columbus Citizens Foundation, and other leaders of the group did not return messages.

But Angie Markham, executive director of FAIO of Queens, which organizes the Astoria event, said Mamdani not attending the Astoria parade “isn’t gonna make or break the event for me.”

“People wanna change history,” she said. “It is what it is. This is the day we chose to [honor] Italian heritage. The Spanish have a whole month. The blacks have a whole month. We have one day. Leave us alone!”

Jerry Iannece, a criminal court judge and parade chairman, said Mamdani and other far-left pols’ disdain for Columbus is “misguided,” adding that “there’s a lot of people who want to rewrite history.”

Carlo Scissura, vice chairman of the FAIO of Brooklyn, declined to address Mamdani’s snub at the Bensonhurst parade but said, “We are proud and excited to host our annual parade, a powerful celebration of Italian American heritage, pride and culture.”

Many Brooklyn patrons said they were upset — but not shocked — Mamdani snubbed Big Apple Italian Americans yet again.

“It’s very disappointing because we elected him the mayor, and he is supposed to be representing everybody,” said Albert Esposito, 72, a retired school teacher.

“It’s a slap in the face to the Italian American community,” said Paul DeSpirito, 53, who runs a neighborhood Italian sandwich and catering business.

Others said they were glad Mamdani was a no-show.

“F– you! He wouldn’t be welcomed,” ripped one man who wanted to remain anonymous.

The Mayor’s Office did not immediately return messages.

The mayor came under fire in July after his administration left Little Italy — along with other beloved ethnic neighborhoods — off a newly released city map of immigrant enclaves despite it being a nationally recognized historic district.

Mamdani insisted the list wasn’t “exhaustive” and said future versions would be amended to include Little Italy. But the friction with Italian Americans goes back further.

A Mamdani social media post from 2020 surfaced during last year’s mayoral race showing the Ugandan-born pol flipping the bird to the Christopher Columbus statue in Astoria. Mamdani, who that same year successfully ran to represent the neighborhood in the state Assembly, included the caption, “Take it down.”

Council Speaker Julie Menin, a moderate Democrat whom Mamdani has repeatedly clashed with while trying to push his far-left agenda, was grand marshal at the Brooklyn parade.
